title: Strangers and Exiles: Christians as Resident Aliens
lead: The Bible pictures God's people as foreigners on the earth: Abraham a resident alien in Canaan, Israel living on God's land as his tenants, the faithful of Hebrews 11 seeking a country in heaven, and in 1 Peter believers who are 'resident aliens and temporary residents'. Early Christian letters greet churches that 'live as resident aliens' in their cities, and the Epistle to Diognetus makes the idea a portrait of Christian life: at home everywhere and nowhere, citizens of heaven.

sections.b: Abraham tells the people of Hebron, 'I am a foreigner living among you as a settler' (Genesis 23:4). The Law gives Israel the same standing before God: 'the land is mine. You are foreigners and lodgers living with me' (Leviticus 25:23). David prays, 'we are foreigners before you, and lodgers, as all our fathers were' (1 Chronicles 29:15), and a psalmist, 'I am a foreigner with you, / a lodger, as all my fathers were' (Psalm 39:12). Israel's law on the resident foreigner among them is on the page Foreigners and the People of God; the loss of the land is on the page Exile.

Hebrews says the patriarchs 'admitted that they were foreigners and temporary residents on the earth' (Hebrews 11:13), because 'they are reaching for a better one, a country in heaven' (Hebrews 11:16); 'We do not have a city here that remains' (Hebrews 13:14). Paul tells the Philippians, citizens of a Roman colony, 'we belong to a commonwealth in heaven' (Philippians 3:20), and 1 Peter writes to 'the chosen temporary residents of the Dispersion' (1 Peter 1:1): 'live in fear during your time as resident aliens' (1 Peter 1:17); 'as resident aliens and temporary residents, keep away from the flesh's desires' (1 Peter 2:11). Ephesians gives the other side: Gentile believers are 'no longer strangers and resident aliens' but 'citizens together with the saints' (Ephesians 2:19). Jeremiah's letter to the exiles, 'Seek the peace of the city I sent you to' (Jeremiah 29:7), shows how such foreigners are to live meanwhile.
sections.refs: Hebrews 11:9-16; Hebrews 13:14; Philippians 3:20; 1 Peter 1:1; 1 Peter 1:17; 1 Peter 2:11; Ephesians 2:19; Jeremiah 29:7

sections.b: Early Christian letters (1 Clement, Polycarp to the Philippians, the Martyrdom of Polycarp) open with the same word. 'The church of God that lives as a resident alien in Rome, to the church of God that lives as a resident alien in Corinth' (1 Clement 1:0); Polycarp writes 'to the church of God that lives as a resident alien in Philippi' (Polycarp to the Philippians 1:0); Smyrna writes to Philomelium in the same way (Martyrdom of Polycarp 1:0). Each local church is a colony of foreigners whose home is in heaven.
sections.refs: 1 Clement 1:0; Polycarp to the Philippians 1:0; Martyrdom of Polycarp 1:0

sections.b: The Epistle to Diognetus works the picture out at length. Christians 'live in their own homelands, but as resident aliens. They take part in everything as citizens, and they put up with everything as strangers. Every foreign land is their homeland, and every homeland is a foreign land' (Epistle to Diognetus 5:5). 'They pass their days on earth, but they live as citizens of heaven' (Epistle to Diognetus 5:9); they obey the laws and outdo them (Epistle to Diognetus 5:10); they 'live as resident aliens among things that perish' while they wait for incorruption (Epistle to Diognetus 6:8). The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes 5:5 and 5:10 in its teaching on the duties of citizens (2240).
sections.refs: Epistle to Diognetus 5:1-10; Epistle to Diognetus 6:8; Epistle to Diognetus 10:7
